analysis.one_liner: Bars federal health programs from buying drugs with Chinese-made ingredients and gives drugmakers tax breaks to manufacture in the US.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2020 with a Republican sponsor and 11 cosponsors, referred to four House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced during the early COVID-19 pandemic, would have required the government to publish a registry showing where critical drugs and their ingredients are made, and to label drugs with the country of origin of each active ingredient. It would have phased out federal health programs — Medicare, Medicaid, the VA, and military health care — buying drugs whose active ingredients come from China, first requiring 60% non-Chinese ingredients by 2022 and 100% by 2023, with limited waivers before 2025. To make reshoring possible, it offered drug and medical device companies a 100% immediate tax write-off for new or expanded US manufacturing plants through 2025. It never advanced past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would benefit US drug and medical device manufacturers, who would gain a 100% tax write-off on new domestic plants and a guaranteed shift of federal purchasing toward non-Chinese ingredients. Patients in federal health programs would gain supply-chain transparency through country-of-origin labeling and a public registry of critical foreign-made drugs, and would face less exposure to supply disruptions traced to a single country — though only if alternative suppliers could actually fill the gap.

how_it_helps.text: It requires HHS to keep a public registry of critical drugs made abroad, including which ones depend on Chinese ingredients and what each step of their supply chain looks like.
It requires drug labels to state the country of origin of every active ingredient, so patients and buyers can see where their medicine comes from.
It bars federal health programs from buying drugs whose active ingredients come from China — 60% by 2022, 100% by 2023 — with limited waivers.
It gives companies a 100% immediate tax deduction for building or expanding drug and medical device manufacturing plants in the United States through 2025.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new tax breaks through reduced federal revenue, and Medicare, Medicaid, VA, and military health programs could pay more for drugs if suppliers without Chinese ingredients charge higher prices. If alternative ingredient sources were not built in time, patients in federal programs could face shortages of essential medicines.

drawbacks.text: Requiring all federal health programs to buy drugs with 100% non-Chinese ingredients by 2023, with no waivers allowed after 2024, could cause shortages of essential medicines if no alternative suppliers existed — a particular risk for low-cost generics where China dominates ingredient production.

The bill's tax provision lets drug and medical device makers immediately write off the full cost of new or expanded US manufacturing facilities through 2025, a federal subsidy to a profitable industry whose cost is borne by taxpayers through reduced revenue.

Shifting procurement away from the lowest-cost suppliers could raise what Medicare, Medicaid, the VA, and the Department of Defense pay for drugs, a cost ultimately passed to taxpayers and beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — making the medicine supply for federal health programs less dependent on China — was a serious one, and the country-of-origin labeling and registry would have given Americans information they do not have today. But the strongest objection is real: China supplies a large share of the world's generic drug ingredients, and the bill required a full switch within roughly two years, with waivers unavailable after 2024. If replacement suppliers were not ready, the law could have produced shortages of essential medicines. The 100% expensing tax break was also uncapped and tilted toward large manufacturers, adding federal borrowing. On balance the bill addressed a genuine vulnerability but with a timeline and leverage that many in the industry and health agencies would likely have pushed to soften.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2020 and referred to four House committees, including a health subcommittee, but no committee ever acted on it and the full House never voted, so it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 10, 2020 and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs Committees.

Its only further movement was a referral to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee in July 2020 and to the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee that same day; no hearings, markup, or floor vote followed.
The bill never attracted a Democratic cosponsor; its sponsor and 11 cosponsors were all House Republicans.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not passed by then expire and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: drugmakers importing Chinese-made ingredients faced no new procurement restrictions, and manufacturers got no tax break either. Members of the House who chose not to act were spared a vote on a measure that could raise federal drug costs or cause shortages.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing drug supply-chain status quo

for.name: 11 of 197 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Liz Cheney, Elise Stefanik, and Ted Budd
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Democrat signed on.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape beyond sponsorship is unknown.

industries.industry: US pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill offered a 100% immediate tax deduction for new or expanded US manufacturing plants and would push federal health programs toward domestically sourced ingredients, creating a guaranteed customer base for reshored production. It never passed, so the benefit never arrived.

industries.industry: Drugmakers relying on Chinese active ingredients (generic manufacturers)
industries.note: Many low-cost generic drugs depend on Chinese active ingredients; the procurement ban would have forced these makers to restructure supply chains or lose federal program sales. Compliance costs could translate into higher drug prices for everyone.

The bill's core purpose was to cut these suppliers out of the federal drug market entirely by 2023. As a formal trade restriction on a named country, it was as much a geopolitical measure as a health one.

industries.industry: Medicare, Medicaid, VA, and military health beneficiaries
industries.note: Patients in federal programs stood to gain supply-chain security and transparency, but bore the risk of shortages during the transition and potentially higher drug costs if alternatives were more expensive.
